newsitem.title: USA: Working mothers see gains in U.S. companies.
newsitem.headline: Working mothers see gains in U.S. companies.

text.p: One hundred U.S. companies were praised on Tuesday for balancing work and family life by recognising child care needs, adopting flexible schedules and offering paid leave for new fathers and adoptive parents.
The 11th annual report by WorkingMother magazine said women were gaining stature in the workplace and many of the 100 firms offered reduced work time to take care of a child.
Alternative work options for employees and paid maternity leave were the norm among the 100 companies, while 23 firms gave paid leave to new fathers and 75 had child care centres.

Vice President Al Gore, keynote speaker at the magazine's annual awards to the "100 best companies for working mothers," said businesses that helped employees in their lives received loyalty and higher quality work in return.

The magazine listed the 10 best companies as Barnett Banks, Eli Lilly, Hewlett-Packard, IBM, Johnson & Johnson, MBNA America Bank, Merck, NationsBank, Patagonia and Xerox. It said 17 firms were on its list for the first time, including Wall Street giants Bankers Trust and Merrill Lynch.
Gore asked representatives of the 100 companies -- many of them chief executive officers and chief financial officers -- to urge other firms to adopt "family-friendly" policies.

"A shocking number of companies still do not let themselves look far enough into their own future," he said. "We need national policies that speed up this new learning, speed up this evolution in the workplace."

President Clinton and Gore are running their reelection campaign partly on family issues and the vice-president said it was "not an accident" that the first piece of legislation Clinton signed into law was the Family and Medical Leave Act.

Gore, who has been positioning himself for his own presidential bid in four years, said people had taken advantage of the rights bestowed by the act on 12 million occasions and the Clinton administration wanted to expand it.

"For those who said that the act and other family-friendly policies hurt the economy, it certainly has not," he said. New jobs had been created, unemployment was down, more small businesses had opened and inflation was at a 30-year low.
